The problem concerns a quantum particle confined to a one-dimensional infinite potential well of width \(a\). Such a system is among the most elementary exactly solvable models in introductory quantum mechanics, and it serves as a useful test bed for understanding how stationary-state wavefunctions encode information about position and momentum observables. In part (a), the question asks for the expectation value of the \(x\)-component of momentum when the particle occupies the \(n=1\) stationary state. In part (b), it asks for the probability of locating the particle in the central third of the box for the ground state and the first two excited states.

A careful treatment must begin by specifying the domain and boundary conditions. For an infinite well, the potential is zero inside the interval \(0 < x < a\) and infinite elsewhere, which forces the wavefunction to vanish at the boundaries. The allowed stationary states are standing waves with discrete quantum numbers, and each state possesses a well-defined symmetry about the centre of the well only after an appropriate coordinate shift, though the usual textbook form places the origin at one wall. This choice of origin affects the algebraic appearance of the wavefunctions but not the physical probabilities or expectation values.

For the momentum expectation value, one substitutes the appropriate stationary-state wavefunction into the standard definition of an expectation value, applies the differential momentum operator, and carries out the integration over the well. Because the momentum operator is Hermitian and the probability density of a bound stationary state is time-independent, the resulting expectation value must be real. The standing-wave character of the eigenfunctions—being superpositions of equal-amplitude left- and right-moving components—suggests a balance between positive and negative momentum contributions. A rigorous computation confirms this intuition, and the outcome can be interpreted physically in terms of the symmetry of the state and the absence of a preferred direction of motion.

For the position-probability questions, the relevant quantity is the integral of the probability density over the specified subinterval. One substitutes the appropriate stationary-state wavefunction, exploits standard trigonometric identities to reduce the squared trigonometric term, and evaluates the resulting elementary integrals between the given limits. The symmetry of the probability distribution about the midpoint of the well implies that the probability in the central third is not determined by the length of the interval alone; rather, it depends on the nodal structure of the particular excited state. As the quantum number increases, the probability density oscillates more rapidly, and the integrated probability in any fixed finite subinterval approaches the behaviour expected in the classical limit.

Practitioners typically approach these calculations by first writing down the normalized eigenfunctions, then performing the integrals either analytically or with the aid of symmetry arguments. Common pitfalls include forgetting normalization factors, misapplying the momentum operator, or overlooking the distinction between probability density and probability amplitude. Care must also be taken with the limits of integration and with the conversion of trigonometric arguments. Overall, the problem is a straightforward illustration of how the formalism of quantum mechanics connects measurable quantities to the properties of stationary-state wavefunctions.

Assume, in search of a contradiction, that \(\mu_k\) is larger than \(\mu_s\). Imagine pushing a block that rests on a surface. If the applied force is smaller than \(\mu_s N\) (such as the force indicated by the point A on the scale in Fig. 4.35), then nothing happens. The static friction exactly cancels the applied force, and the block just sits there.

However, if the applied force lies between \(\mu_s N\) and \(\mu_k N\) (such as the force indicated by the point B), then we have problem. On one hand, the applied force exceeds \(\mu_s N\) (which is the maximum static friction force, by definition), so the block should move. But on the other hand, the applied force is smaller than the kinetic friction force, \(\mu_k N\), so the block shouldn’t move. Basically, as soon as the block moves even the slightest infinitesimal amount (at which point the kinetic friction force becomes the relevant force), it will decelerate and stop because the kinetic friction force wins out over the applied force. So it actually never moves at all, even for the applied force represented by point B. This means, by the definition of \(\mu_s\), that \(\mu_s N\) is actually located higher than point B. The above contradiction (where the block both does move and doesn’t move) will arise unless \(\mu_s N \ge \mu_k N\). So we conclude that it must be the case that \(\mu_s \ge \mu_k\). There then exists no point B below \(\mu_k N\) and above \(\mu_s N\).

In the real world, \(\mu_s\) is rarely larger than twice \(\mu_k\). In some cases the two are essentially equal, with \(\mu_s\) being a hair larger.

In the setting of severe malnutrition, the preservation of cognitive function in a child presents a striking clinical paradox. If higher neurological processes remain intact despite profound depletion of systemic nutrient stores, one is compelled to ask what property of cerebral glucose uptake permits the brain to continue operating when the rest of the body is energy-starved. The question directs our attention not to the quantity of glucose delivered, but to the mechanistic character of the transport step itself—specifically, what molecular feature must be in place to safeguard neuronal metabolism under conditions of generalised nutritional deprivation.

This matter carries considerable physiological and clinical weight. The brain is an obligate consumer of glucose under ordinary conditions, and its metabolic demand is both continuous and exquisitely sensitive to interruption. In a well-nourished state, multiple endocrine pathways cooperate to maintain glycaemic stability, and the transport of glucose into peripheral tissues is tightly coupled to hormonal signalling. Severe malnutrition, however, disrupts the usual endocrine milieu: circulating nutrient levels fall, anabolic drive diminishes, and the hormonal cues that ordinarily facilitate substrate uptake into muscle and adipose tissue become blunted or absent. That the brain should continue to function under such circumstances implies that its glucose acquisition pathway does not depend on the very signals that are failing elsewhere.

A careful consideration of this problem therefore requires distinguishing between transport modalities that are regulated by systemic endocrine status and those that are constitutive or autoregulated. The central issue is the nature of the dependence relationship: whether glucose entry into the cerebral compartment is conditional upon a hormonal trigger, or whether it proceeds as a function of local substrate availability and transporter intrinsic activity. Where uptake is contingent upon a signal that is itself suppressed in malnutrition, one would anticipate a breakdown of cerebral metabolism and consequent cognitive decline; the absence of such decline argues strongly for a transport mechanism whose operation is insulated from that signal.

Several additional considerations refine the analysis. First, the blood–brain barrier introduces a discrete compartment: glucose must traverse the endothelial interface before reaching the neuroparenchyma, and the transport step at this interface may be governed by different molecular logic than uptake into neurons themselves. Second, the affinity and capacity of the relevant transporters matter, since low ambient glucose concentrations require high-affinity capture to sustain flux. Third, one must consider whether the system is merely insensitive to hormonal variation or actively upregulated in response to substrate deprivation—though the clinical scenario does not require the latter, only that the rate-limiting step not be blocked by endocrine failure. Edge cases include sepsis or refeeding states, where transporter regulation may shift unpredictably and complicate the inference.

Practitioners approaching this question in clinical pathology typically reason from first principles of tissue-specific substrate handling, contrasting the hormonal responsiveness of peripheral tissues with the constancy demanded by neuronal metabolism. The emphasis falls on identifying which functional category of transport—hormone-dependent or otherwise—would remain competent when systemic endocrine tone is depressed and circulating glucose is scarce. In sum, the critical attribute lies in the transport mechanism’s relationship to the principal anabolic hormone, and determining that relationship resolves the apparent paradox of preserved cognition in the face of profound systemic depletion.

# Evaluation of Acid-Base Status in Salicylate Toxicity

The interpretation of an arterial blood gas panel in the setting of suspected salicylate exposure is a cornerstone of toxicologic assessment, because the electrochemical signature carried in the blood often heralds clinical deterioration before overt symptoms become unmistakable. The scenario presented—pH, pCO₂, and bicarbonate values drawn from a patient with known salicylic acid poisoning—demands a disciplined, stepwise reading of each variable and of the relationships among them rather than a quick pattern-match to a single label. Accuracy here matters profoundly: misreading the disturbance can misdirect therapy toward inadequate alkalinisation, inappropriate ventilation, or delayed haemodialysis.

Salicylates disturb acid-base homeostasis through several simultaneous mechanisms. At the mitochondrial level, they uncouple oxidative phosphorylation, accelerating substrate utilisation and generating heat and organic acid intermediates. They also directly stimulate the medullary respiratory centre, increasing minute ventilation independent of, and often in excess of, the prevailing metabolic need. Any rigorous interpretation must therefore remain alert to the possibility that more than one primary process is unfolding concurrently, and that the numerical values may not be reducible to a simple, single-axis disturbance.

A careful treatment of the question would involve several interlocking layers of reasoning. The clinician would first locate the pH on the acid-base spectrum and determine whether the net acid-base balance tilts toward acidaemia or alkalaemia. Attention would then turn to the carbon dioxide tension and the bicarbonate concentration, asking whether each is shifted in a direction consistent with a primary respiratory process, a primary metabolic process, or both. The next analytic move is the evaluation of compensation: whether the non-primary system has moved in the expected direction and, crucially, whether it has moved by an amount congruent with a purely compensatory response or whether its magnitude suggests an independent, coexisting primary disorder. In salicylate intoxication, this last judgement is where many interpretations falter, because the respiratory drive imposed by the toxin can far exceed the degree of ventilation that simple metabolic compensation would predict.

Several caveats deserve emphasis. Temporal evolution is critical: early after ingestion, one pattern may predominate, while later, as lactate and ketone accumulation intensifies, the metabolic component may deepen and obscure the original respiratory contribution. Concurrent ingestions, pre-existing pulmonary or renal disease, and therapeutic interventions such as bicarbonate infusion or mechanical ventilation can each distort the picture. Practitioners also consider whether the anion gap, the delta-delta relationship, and the serum electrolytes are available to corroborate the inference drawn from the blood gas alone, since these adjunctive data often clarify whether a mixed disorder is truly present or whether an apparent anomaly is an artefact of measurement or of isolated sampling.

In routine practice, experienced clinicians resist the temptation to collapse the analysis into a phrase before each variable has been interrogated individually and in concert. They hold the competing mechanisms salicylates exert—respiratory stimulation and metabolic acid generation—in mind simultaneously, allowing the data to reveal whether one, both, or neither is the dominant feature in the patient before them. This disciplined, mechanistic approach is what transforms a blood gas from a collection of numbers into an actionable physiologic narrative.

The mass spectrum of molecular bromine presents an elegant textbook case for extracting isotopic information from a small set of peak positions and intensities. Because the molecule is diatomic and composed of a single element, the combinatorial structure of the peaks is tightly constrained: with two contributing isotopes, the spectrum can display at most three distinct molecular masses, corresponding to the three possible pairings. The relative intensities of those peaks, in turn, encode the per-isotope abundance ratio, while the peak positions themselves encode the atomic masses. The task, then, is to invert these observables consistently.

A rigorous treatment begins by assigning each of the three observed peaks to a specific isotopologue. The heaviest peak corresponds to the molecule composed of the heavier isotope in both atomic positions; the lightest, to the lighter isotope in both positions; and the central peak to the mixed combination. This assignment follows from the additive nature of atomic masses in a diatomic molecule. Once that mapping is fixed, the two atomic masses can be read directly from the lightest and heaviest peak positions, since each is simply twice the respective atomic mass. The mixed peak provides a useful consistency check, as it should equal the arithmetic mean of the two homogeneous peaks.

The abundance analysis proceeds from the binomial expansion. For a population of identical atoms drawn from two isotopic species with fractional abundances \(p\) and \(1-p\), randomly paired into molecules, the expected proportions of the three molecular species take the ordered form associated with coefficients of \((p + (1-p))^2\). Matching these ordered theoretical proportions to the observed relative sizes yields the individual isotopic abundances. It is worth noting that the two homogeneous peaks each involve the same abundance factor squared, while the mixed peak involves twice the product of the two factors; this structural feature gives the central peak its characteristic prominence when the two abundances are comparable.

With the atomic masses and fractional abundances in hand, the average atomic mass follows as the abundance-weighted sum of the isotope masses. The average molecular mass of \(\mathrm{Br_2}\) is then simply twice that quantity, or equivalently the corresponding weighted combination over the three molecular peaks. Both routes should agree, and cross-checking them is good practice.

Several practical considerations deserve mention. Peak positions in real spectra carry finite instrumental uncertainty, so the extracted masses should be reported to an appropriate number of significant figures rather than over-precisely. Relative intensities depend on detection efficiency and may require normalization, though here they have already been presented as proportions summing to unity. Finally, one should verify that the reported intensities are internally consistent with a single common abundance parameter; any significant discrepancy would suggest either measurement error or the presence of additional unresolved species. In the present case, the data appear clean, and the standard two-isotope model is fully adequate for the analysis.

The evaluation of acute or recurrent scrotal swelling in a young child is a clinical scenario that demands careful attention to history, physical examination findings, and an understanding of the developmental anatomy of the inguinal canal. In the case presented—a 3-year-old with red scrotal swelling that resolves by the following morning, worsens in the evening, and demonstrates a positive transillumination test—the clinician must integrate several converging pieces of evidence to arrive at a coherent explanation. The key observations are the positional and temporal variability of the swelling, the fluid nature of the scrotal contents as indicated by transillumination, and the age of the patient, all of which focus the differential diagnosis within a relatively narrow band of congenital and developmental conditions.

Why this presentation matters is that pediatric scrotal swelling, while often benign, can occasionally signal a surgical emergency. The possibility of testicular torsion, incarcerated hernia, or other acute processes must always be consciously excluded before considering more indolent causes. The history that the swelling resolves overnight and worsens in the evening is a particularly important clue, because it suggests a dynamic process in which the contents of the scrotum change in response to posture and gravitational forces. This pattern contrasts with the fixed, persistent swelling typical of solid masses, hematomas, or acute inflammatory processes that do not fluctuate with position.

A careful diagnostic approach to this problem involves systematic consideration of several categories of disease. First, conditions involving abnormal communication between the peritoneal cavity and the scrotal compartment must be considered, as such communications allow fluid or other contents to shift depending on intra-abdominal pressure and patient position. Second, non-communicating fluid collections must be evaluated; these tend to be stable in size rather than fluctuating. Third, acute inflammatory or infectious causes, such as epididymitis or orchitis, must be weighed, though these typically present with pain, fever, or systemic symptoms rather than with swelling that spontaneously resolves. Inguinal hernias represent another category, particularly those that reduce spontaneously, though transillumination findings and the absence of a palpable bowel loop in the scrotum would influence interpretation.

The positive transillumination test is a valuable bedside finding that helps classify the swelling as fluid-filled rather than solid. Transillumination is performed by shining a light source through the swollen tissue; a fluid collection generally transmits light diffusely, whereas solid tissue does not. This finding narrows the differential but does not, in isolation, establish a diagnosis, because several fluid-containing scrotal processes may yield similar results. The color of the overlying skin—described here as red—can represent dependent erythema from vascular congestion, mild reactive inflammation, or simple skin irritation, and must be interpreted in conjunction with the remainder of the examination.

Practitioners typically approach such presentations by combining history with a focused physical examination performed both when the child is upright and when supine. Observing whether the swelling changes in size with crying, straining, or changes in position provides essential diagnostic information. Ultrasonography may be employed when uncertainty remains, though in straightforward cases the clinical history and examination often suffice to guide management decisions. Caveats include the possibility of ambiguity between reducible hernias and fluid collections that shift position, as well as the rare occurrence of concomitant pathology. Ultimately, the goal is to distinguish conditions that require surgical intervention from those that may be observed, ensuring that the child receives appropriate follow-up without unnecessary intervention.

**Clinical Framing and Pathophysiological Context**

The presentation described—tachypnea, hepatomegaly, and echocardiographic findings of asymmetric septal hypertrophy in an infant of a diabetic mother—calls for a structured cardiac evaluation within the broader differential of neonatal and early infant cardiomyopathies. The history of maternal diabetes is a key epidemiological clue, as in utero hyperinsulinemia and altered substrate delivery can imprint persistent ventricular remodeling. The asymmetric septal hypertrophy observed here is classically linked to transient hypertrophic physiology, which may produce dynamic left ventricular outflow tract obstruction and, when severe, secondary pulmonary congestion and hepatic engorgement. Recognizing this mechanistic chain is essential because it shifts the therapeutic focus away from inotropic support and toward strategies that reduce the dynamic gradient and improve diastolic filling.

**General Principles of Management**

When approaching an infant with this profile, the clinician must weigh several overlapping priorities. First, one must confirm that the echocardiographic morphology is isolated and not superimposed on a congenital malformation or metabolic cardiomyopathy, as management diverges substantially. Second, symptom severity—degree of respiratory distress, feeding intolerance, and evidence of low cardiac output—guides the intensity of intervention. Third, the natural history of this condition often includes spontaneous regression of the hypertrophic substrate over the first year of life; therefore, any pharmacological choice should mitigate acute hemodynamic burden without provoking adverse remodeling or delaying physiologic involution.

A careful treatment plan would typically involve selecting an agent that lowers heart rate, attenuates systolic hypercontractility, and thereby reduces the systolic anterior motion–mediated obstruction. The aim is to improve net forward flow and relieve venous congestion, all while preserving adequate perfusion and avoiding hypotension. Volume status must be monitored closely because relative hypovolemia can exacerbate dynamic obstruction, whereas overload worsens pulmonary congestion. Additionally, any concurrent electrolyte or glucose disturbance—especially relevant given the maternal diabetic background—should be corrected to avoid superimposed arrhythmia or contractile instability.

**Caveats and Usual Practice**

Practitioners generally approach these infants with a staged mindset: supportive stabilization first, pharmacologic attenuation of hypercontractility if symptomatic obstruction is present, and serial echocardiographic follow-up to document regression. In severe, refractory cases, escalation to more invasive modalities may be considered, though this is uncommon. It is also important to counsel caregivers regarding expected timeline and to coordinate follow-up with pediatric cardiology. Ultimately, the decision rests on integrating the echocardiographic gradient, clinical signs of congestion, and the infant’s growth trajectory, ensuring that the chosen therapy aligns with the anticipated transient nature of the hypertrophy while providing symptomatic relief during the vulnerable early months.

The question posed sits at an instructive boundary in stellar physics: the precise threshold separating non-fusing substellar objects from objects capable of sustained hydrogen burning. At face value it asks whether a minuscule mass increment, just over a kilogram, can push a body sitting immediately below the hydrogen-burning limit into an active phase of stellar fusion, and whether the subsequent loss of that same increment through fusion products would then return the object to its prior substellar state. Resolving the scenario requires care, because the phrasing implicitly treats the mass threshold as a clean, static line and treats fusion as a process whose mass-loss timescale is comparable to the mass increment itself. Both assumptions deserve scrutiny.

A rigorous treatment would begin by recalling that the hydrogen-burning minimum mass is not a universal constant but a function of composition, particularly metallicity and helium fraction, and is sensitive to the equation of state and opacity in the stellar interior. The threshold is conventionally established through models of fully convective objects in hydrostatic equilibrium, in which the central temperature rises with increasing mass until the pp-chain reaction rate becomes sufficient to offset radiative losses. One would therefore need to specify whether the additional mass preserves composition, whether it is delivered in a manner consistent with hydrostatic equilibrium, and over what timescale the accretion occurs, since rapid addition could transiently perturb the thermal structure.

A further consideration is the characteristic timescale of stellar mass loss through nuclear fusion. The conversion of hydrogen to helium releases energy according to the mass-energy equivalence, but the fraction of rest mass converted in proton-proton chain reactions is extremely small, and the luminosity of an object near the minimum mass is low. Consequently, the timescale over which fusion measurably reduces the total mass is enormously long compared with the magnitude of the mass increment in question. Any argument about the object returning to a substellar state after losing a comparable mass must engage this disparity in timescales directly.

Practitioners approaching such a problem would typically construct or consult evolutionary tracks for low-mass objects, comparing the thermal and nuclear timescales at masses just above and below the effective burning limit. They would also distinguish between the ignition of fusion, which may occur even below the canonical minimum mass in a transient sense, and the sustained burning that defines a main-sequence star. Caveats include the role of deuterium burning, which proceeds at lower masses and is irrelevant to long-term hydrogen ignition but can confuse discussions of “burning,” as well as the possibility that a body exactly at the threshold exhibits a long-lived but ultimately finite active phase.

In summary, the problem is best approached by comparing the nuclear timescale associated with the added mass against both the thermal timescale of the envelope and the main-sequence lifetime appropriate to an object of this mass regime. Only such a comparative analysis can adjudicate between the two proposed outcomes.

responses.text:
The observation that male and female offspring differ uniformly in phenotype, with every male green and every female yellow, immediately signals that a straightforward autosomal model will not suffice. Whenever a trait partitions cleanly by sex in the first generation, the investigator is directed toward sex-linked inheritance as the organising principle. The question therefore asks us not merely to label the phenomenon but to identify the specific chromosomal regime—homogametic versus heterogametic sex, and which parent carries which allele—that generates the observed pattern.

A careful treatment begins by cataloguing the relevant genetic architecture. In birds, sex determination follows the ZW system, which differs from the more familiar XY mammalian pattern: males are typically the homogametic sex and females the heterogametic one. Any discussion of plumage colour in canaries must keep this asymmetry at the forefront, because the direction of cross transmission depends entirely on which sex carries two identical sex chromosomes and which carries two different ones. Equally important is the observation that all offspring within each sex class are phenotypically identical. Uniformity of this kind rules out heterozygosity among the parents for the locus in question; had either parent been heterozygous, one would expect at least two phenotypes to appear within at least one sex class. Thus the data point to homozygous or hemizygous parents, which sharply constrains the range of viable models.

Practitioners confronted with such a cross usually proceed by explicit hypothesis testing. One first sets up the cross under the default or assumed sex-determination system, assigns alleles to the parental genotypes, and traces segregation into the offspring. If the predicted phenotypes match the data, the problem is resolved; if they do not, the next step is to reverse the assumption about which sex is homogametic and repeat the analysis. The power of this approach lies in its exhaustiveness: by systematically swapping roles and re-deriving expectations, one can identify the unique configuration consistent with observation. Along the way, several caveats deserve attention. Lethality of certain sex-chromosome combinations could distort ratios, though the presence of both sexes among offspring argues against complete lethality. Similarly, incomplete penetrance or environmental effects on pigment deposition might blur expectations, yet the crisp one-to-one correspondence between sex and colour in these data leaves little room for such modifiers. responses.text:
The zipper model is a beautifully stripped-down stat-mechanical description of DNA denaturation, in which the double helix is represented as an ordered sequence of base-pair links that unzip only from one end. The restriction that a link may flip only when all links to its left are open and all to its right are closed reduces the configuration space dramatically, converting a combinatorial problem into one essentially governed by a single ordering coordinate. The task is to find the equilibrium thermal average of that coordinate—the mean number of open links—and to understand how it behaves across the full temperature range, paying special attention to the thermodynamic limit of very long chains.

This problem is instructive because it sits at the intersection of elementary statistical mechanics and the physics of cooperative sequential processes. The energy cost is linear in the number of open links, so the Hamiltonian is simple; the nontriviality comes entirely from the constrained geometry and the finite size of the chain. A careful treatment begins by enumerating the admissible configurations, assigning each its Boltzmann weight, and forming the partition function. Because the allowed states are naturally indexed by an integer ranging from zero to the chain length, the partition function reduces to a finite geometric sum. The desired average is then the ratio of a derivative-weighted sum to the partition sum itself, a standard device in equilibrium statistical mechanics. One may evaluate both sums in closed form, after which the temperature dependence can be read off directly from the resulting expression.

Several limiting regimes deserve comment. At temperatures far below the characteristic link energy, excitation of even the first link is strongly suppressed, and the chain remains almost entirely closed. At the opposite extreme, when thermal energy overwhelms the link cost, the energetic bias becomes negligible and the chain tends toward a symmetric distribution between open and closed configurations. For very long chains there is additionally a broad intermediate regime in which the behavior crosses over smoothly between these two extremes; identifying the length and temperature scales that control this crossover is one of the central goals of the analysis. Practitioners typically obtain these limits by comparing the two competing exponential factors that appear in the exact expression, examining which dominates in each region of the parameter plane.

In approaching the problem one should keep several caveats in mind. The model assumes no interactions beyond the opening energy and no internal degeneracy for open or closed links; it also imposes a strict directional constraint that may not hold in real DNA, where internal loops and multiple forks can appear. The boundary between the intermediate and high-temperature regimes depends on the chain length, so finite-size effects are non-negligible until the thermodynamic limit is taken carefully. nonetheless, for the idealized chain specified in the question the equilibrium average is fully determined by the constraint, the linear energy, and the Gibbs distribution, and its temperature dependence follows from a straightforward, exact analysis of the resulting partition function.

responses.text:
Reducing unwanted reflection from a lens surface is a central problem in optical engineering, since even small surface losses accumulate across multi-element systems and degrade image contrast. The problem at hand concerns a single thin film deposited on a glass substrate, with refractive index intermediate between that of the surrounding medium and the lens glass. The design wavelength is specified in the visible, and the question asks both for the film thickness that minimizes reflected intensity and for the physical reason the minimum does not reach zero.

(a) The governing phenomenon is two-beam interference in a thin transparent layer. When light strikes the coated surface, part reflects from the outer boundary of the film and part reflects from the film–substrate boundary. The two reflected waves superpose, and their relative phase is set by the optical path difference accumulated in traversing the film twice, together with any phase shifts that accompany reflection at each interface. A careful analysis therefore requires identifying the ordering of the refractive indices across the two boundaries, because a reflection at an interface where the index increases produces a half-cycle phase change, whereas a reflection where the index decreases does not. Once the phase budget is established, the condition for destructive interference in the reflected field fixes the permissible optical thicknesses. The smallest non-zero thickness satisfying that condition gives the minimum coating thickness sought by the problem. Practitioners routinely express the allowed thicknesses as fractions of the design wavelength inside the film, but the explicit evaluation depends on the precise phase shifts present in this particular three-index configuration.

(b) Even when the two reflected waves are made fully out of phase, the resultant intensity will not vanish unless their amplitudes are also equal. The amplitude of each reflected wave is governed by the Fresnel reflection coefficient at its respective interface, which depends on the index contrast. With the film index given, the two boundaries generally have different contrast ratios, so the reflected amplitudes are mismatched and a residual reflected intensity remains. To drive the reflection to zero, one must adjust the film’s refractive index so that the reflection amplitudes from the two interfaces become equal. In the simplest normal-incidence, lossless model this leads to a definite compatibility condition relating the film index to the indices of the surrounding medium and the substrate. Satisfying that condition eliminates the amplitude mismatch, allowing true destructive interference to extinguish the net reflected beam.

Several assumptions underlie this treatment: normal incidence, monochromatic illumination, and ideal, non-absorbing media with sharp interfaces. In practice, coatings must also contend with dispersion over finite bandwidth, oblique incidence, and adhesion or surface roughness, which is why multilayer designs and transfer-matrix calculations are often employed for broadband antireflection performance.
